english: I miss my country.
tip: 'Manquer à' is reversed from English: 'Mon pays me manque' = My country is missing to me = I miss my country. The thing missed is subject.

english: This man is friendly.
tip: 'Cet' is used before masculine nouns starting with a vowel or silent 'h': cet homme, cet arbre, cet hôtel.

english: Hello, how are you?
tip: 'Bonjour' is used from morning to evening. Use 'bonsoir' after around 6 pm. 'Comment allez-vous ?' is formal.

english: See you later (same day).
tip: 'À tout à l'heure' = see you later (today). 'À plus tard' = see you later (less specific). 'À bientôt' = see you soon.

english: The weather is nice today.
tip: Weather uses 'il fait' + adjective: il fait beau (nice), il fait chaud (hot), il fait froid (cold), il fait mauvais (bad).

english: I need to rest.
tip: You don't 'need' something in French, you 'have need of' it: avoir besoin de. 'J'ai besoin de me reposer' is literally 'I have need of resting.' The 'de' is never optional.

english: For here, please.
tip: 'Sur place' literally means 'on the spot' and is how you say eating in, not takeaway. At a café you'll hear 'sur place ou à emporter?' = for here or to go?

english: I really like this movie.
tip: 'Plaire à' has a reverse construction: the thing liked is the subject. 'Ce film me plaît' = This movie pleases me (= I like this movie).

english: Do you like it here?
tip: The easiest question needs no extra words: keep normal order and raise your voice. 'Ça te plaît ici ?' is a statement asked with a rising tone.

english: Do you like it? (formal)
tip: 'Vous' here is formal singular. In formal French, always use 'vous' with strangers and superiors.

english: My son is three years old.
tip: You HAVE your age in French: mon fils a trois ans is literally 'my son has three years.' Never use être for age.

english: I can't wait to see you again.
tip: 'Avoir hâte de' = to look forward to, literally 'to have haste to.' 'J'ai hâte de te revoir' = I can't wait to see you again. The impatience is a thing you possess, not a feeling.

english: I would like a glass of water.
tip: 'Je voudrais' (conditional of vouloir) is the polite way to say 'I would like'. More polite than 'je veux' (I want).

target: Il me semble que c'est vrai.
english: It seems to me that it's true.
tip: 'Il me semble que' = It seems to me that. 'Sembler' uses the same reverse pattern: il me semble, il te semble.

target: La chambre est au deuxième étage.
english: The room is on the second floor.
tip: French floors: rez-de-chaussée (ground floor), premier étage (1st floor = US 2nd floor), deuxième étage (2nd = US 3rd).

target: J'ai mis trois heures pour arriver.
english: It took me three hours to arrive.
tip: Mettre can express duration: j'ai mis + time means it took me + time.

target: Il est blond aux yeux bleus.
english: He is blond with blue eyes.
tip: 'Aux yeux bleus' = with blue eyes. 'Aux' is the contraction of 'à les'. Used for physical descriptions.

target: Elle est brune aux yeux verts.
english: She is brunette with green eyes.
tip: The feminine ending wakes up a silent letter: masculine 'brun' ends silently, but 'brune' sounds the n.

target: Nous dînons en famille le dimanche.
english: We have dinner as a family on Sundays.
tip: 'Le dimanche' with the article means every Sunday, not one particular one: 'Nous dînons en famille le dimanche' = we have dinner as a family on Sundays. Drop the 'le' for a single Sunday.

target: Tu as bu assez d'eau aujourd'hui ?
english: Did you drink enough water today?
tip: Quantity words take plain de, never du or de la: assez d'eau = enough water. Same for beaucoup d'eau, trop d'eau.

target: Dépêche-toi, le train part dans dix minutes!
english: Hurry up, the train leaves in ten minutes!
tip: In a command the reflexive pronoun hops behind the verb and 'te' turns into 'toi': 'Dépêche-toi' = hurry up. Compare the plain statement 'tu te dépêches.'

target: Ça te dit d'aller au cinéma ?
english: Do you feel like going to the movies?
tip: 'Ça te dit de...' = Do you feel like...? Literally 'Does that say to you to...' Another reverse construction.

target: Ils ont pris le train de huit heures.
english: They took the eight o'clock train.
tip: De marks which train by its time: le train de huit heures = the eight o'clock train. It's 'the train of eight hours.'

target: Personne ne connaissait la réponse à cette question.
english: Nobody knew the answer to this question.
tip: 'Personne' means nobody, but it still needs 'ne' before the verb – and no 'pas': 'personne ne connaissait' = nobody knew.

target: Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait, le problème est réglé.
english: No sooner said than done, the problem is solved.
tip: Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait is literally 'as soon as said, as soon as done' – the French for 'no sooner said than done.'

target: Tellement de monde est venu à la fête hier.
english: So many people came to the party yesterday.
tip: Le monde means 'people' here, not 'the world': tellement de monde = so many people. It stays singular, so the verb is est venu.

english: I find this smell unpleasant.
tip: 'Déplaire à' is the opposite of 'plaire à': Ça me déplaît = I don't like that. Same reverse construction.

target: Lentement mais sûrement il apprend à jouer du piano.
english: Slowly but surely he's learning to play the piano.
tip: You play an instrument with 'jouer de,' not plain jouer. 'Jouer du piano' packs de + le into du = to play the piano. Sports flip to jouer à: jouer au foot.

english: Please. (formal)
tip: 'S'il vous plaît' (formal/plural) vs 's'il te plaît' (informal). Literally 'if it pleases you'. Essential polite expression.

english: No problem.
tip: After a negative, French swaps the article for 'de': not 'un problème' but 'pas de problème'. Same with je n'ai pas de temps.
